title: Macaulay Education Policy Impact in Bengal
subtitle: The 1835 English education decision met a varied indigenous school landscape in Bengal; later local effects remain unestablished here.
summary: On 2 February 1835, Macaulay’s Minute argued that government education funds should promote European literature and science through English. Banglapedia describes the Minute and Bentinck’s March resolution as settling the Orientalist–Anglicist dispute in favor of the Anglicists. According to William Adam’s later survey, the selected Bengal districts of Beerbhoom and Burdwan contained 1,041 common schools, while South Behar and Tirhoot contained 365. These are Adam’s counts for selected localities, not a census of Bengal. His reports document the contemporary school landscape and his proposals; they do not establish what the 1835 policy later caused in Bengal.
heroTagline: The policy decision and Adam’s limited survey of indigenous education in Bengal
whyItMatters: Adam’s survey records indigenous schools and differences among the selected districts at the time of the 1835 policy debate. Because he examined only selected localities and warned of gaps in the records, his figures cannot stand for all Bengal. Neither Adam’s reports nor the policy summaries used here establish the later effects of Macaulay’s policy in Bengal; tracing those effects requires local evidence on implementation and change over time.

claimCitations.claim: On 2 February 1835, Macaulay’s Minute argued that government education funds should promote European literature and science through English; Banglapedia describes the decision as resolving the Orientalist–Anglicist dispute in favor of the Anglicists.
In March 1835, Bentinck’s resolution confirmed the Anglicist direction.

According to Adam, the surveyed districts Beerbhoom and Burdwan together had 1,041 common schools, compared with 365 in South Behar and Tirhoot; these are selected-district counts, not a Bengal-wide census.
Adam’s inquiry covered selected districts and one city, and his first report warned that many institutions were unrecorded and local distribution required further investigation.

historicalDebate: Banglapedia describes the 1835 decision as resolving the Orientalist–Anglicist dispute in favor of English education. The sources reviewed here do not establish that the decision immediately abolished indigenous schools or demonstrate its later effects across Bengal. Adam’s reports describe selected places and include his own recommendations; they are not evidence of policy outcomes.
